title: Why one ticket builds 25 chunks
plain: The code uses the Minecraft wiki rule that a forceload ticket is level 31 and each chunk step away adds one, and works out that a 5 by 5 block of chunks ends up fully built; it must match the block we measured.
why: If the published rule predicts the tile we measured, we know why the tile is that size.
done_when: The code gives 25 full chunks, distance 3 is not full, and it equals the saved measurement.

title: The thirteen build stages
plain: The code lists the thirteen stages a chunk goes through, in order, from the 1.16.5 class listing, and checks every stage name we ever saw on disk is on the list.
why: The leftover half-built chunks are only understood once the stages are known.
done_when: All 13 stages are in order and every saved stage name is on the list.

title: What the bug tracker says
plain: Two Mojang bug reports say the world changes with the order chunks are built; the code stores their numbers, dates and a short quote with the link.
why: Claims about earlier knowledge must come with a link and a date.
done_when: The dates match, each quote is under 15 words and every link is present.

title: Which simple rules ignore order
plain: A published paper counts which of the 256 one-line update rules give the same end states in any update order; the code repeats the count on a ring of 5 cells.
why: It is the nearest published count to our question, so we check we read it correctly.
done_when: Exactly 104 of the 256 rules are independent of order.

title: Counting worlds by first ticket
plain: Following Postnikov's paper, the code counts how many different worlds four tickets can make for several kinds of overlap, written fresh and apart from our own counter.
why: Our law says worlds equal corners of a shape; an independent count must agree.
done_when: The counts are 24, 14, 20 and 4 for the four kinds of overlap.

title: The same count by a second rule
plain: Postnikov, Reiner and Williams give a different rule for the same shapes, built from prefixes of an order; the code counts with that rule.
why: Two different rules agreeing is the best evidence the shape reading is right.
done_when: The counts are 24 for every subset and 14 for neighbour runs.

title: Pointing the edges of a graph
plain: Stanley proved that the number of ways to give every edge a direction with no loop of arrows is the chromatic polynomial at minus one; the code counts both ways on small graphs.
why: It is the counting tool if worlds correspond to edge directions of a touching graph.
done_when: The counts 6, 8, 14 and 24 match the polynomial on the four test graphs.

title: Words that may swap letters
plain: Cartier and Foata count words where some letters may swap; the code counts them by brute force and by the formula, for three letters where only two swap.
why: Tickets that cannot affect each other are exactly letters that swap.
done_when: The counts for lengths 0 to 4 are 1, 3, 8, 21, 55 and the formula gives the same.

title: The map of all orders of four
plain: The code builds the map of the 24 orders of four tickets, where one order is below another when it has a subset of its swapped pairs.
why: Classes of orders are easiest to describe as regions of this map.
done_when: The map has 36 neighbour links, layers 1, 3, 5, 6, 5, 3, 1 and one bottom and one top.

title: Are the classes unbroken stretches
plain: A paper on binary search trees says orders that give the same tree form an unbroken stretch of the map; the code checks it for our 14 classes.
why: If classes are unbroken, one run per class plus the borders tells us everything.
done_when: There are 14 classes and each holds every order between any two of its members.

title: Joining cells into pieces
plain: Tarjan's method keeps groups of joined cells; the code checks it on a worked example and against plain flood fill on random graphs.
why: Counting separate regions of the terrain needs a method we trust.
done_when: The example leaves 3 groups of 10 cells and 200 random graphs match flood fill.

title: Pieces minus holes from corners
plain: A standard theorem says corners minus edges plus squares equals pieces minus holes; the code checks it on pictures and on 100 random grids.
why: It gives a second way to check the terrain counts.
done_when: The sums 1, 0 and 2 match on the examples and all 100 random pictures agree.

title: Which hill is older
plain: The method of Edelsbrunner, Letscher and Zomorodian lets the younger of two meeting pieces die; the code runs it on a short list of heights.
why: It is how the cost of joining two regions of terrain is read.
done_when: The pairs are (2, 5) and (3, 6) and one piece born at 1 never dies.

title: Pairing by matrix reduction
plain: The same paper pairs births and deaths by reducing a table of boundaries; the code does it on a hollow square.
why: It gives the loops of the terrain, not only the pieces.
done_when: The corner pairs are (1,4) (2,5) (3,6), one corner never dies and one loop born at 7 never dies.

title: Study numbers meet round 3
plain: The code recounts the number of worlds for each of the 72 saved rows of the round 3 polytope results with Postnikov's counting.
why: A study material only counts if a finding actually uses it.
done_when: All 72 recounts equal the saved class counts.

title: Study tools meet the terrain
plain: The code counts pieces and holes of the seed 7 terrain with the union-find and corner-count code and compares with the saved terrain numbers.
why: It proves our own code agrees with the tool the terrain lane used.
done_when: The code finds 158 pieces and 4 holes, as saved.

title: Every source named, nothing copied
plain: The test checks each study file names its source, quotes stay under 15 words and no paper or book file is in the repo.
why: Papers are not ours to publish.
done_when: All files name a source, no long quote and no paper file exists.

title: The study code stays offline
plain: The test checks no study file reaches for the internet or downloads anything.
why: The study code must give the same answer on any machine.
done_when: No study or test file imports a network library.

title: What the game states
plain: This branch re-derives the facts the game and its bug tracker state about how chunks are built.
why: Our measurements are only as good as our reading of these facts.
done_when: Every leaf under it reaches.

title: The counting maths
plain: This branch re-derives the theorems that count which orders make the same world.
why: The law about orders needs counts we can check by hand.
done_when: Every leaf under it reaches.

title: Reading the terrain
plain: This branch re-derives the tools that read pieces, holes and joining costs of the terrain.
why: The route result stands on these counts.
done_when: Every leaf under it reaches.

title: Used by round 3
plain: This branch ties study code to numbers round 3 already recorded.
why: A material nobody uses is not worth keeping.
done_when: Both bridges reproduce the saved numbers.
